newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Parties torpedo proposed Belgian tax amnesty.
newsitem.headline: Parties torpedo proposed Belgian tax amnesty.

text.p: Belgian government parties on Monday quashed a draft bill to grant those with undeclared cash in foreign bank accounts a so-called one-off fiscal amnesty as long they repatriated their money and invested it locally.
Three of the four parties in the centre-left coalition of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene rejected the idea by Johan Weyts, a senator for Dehaene's christian-democrat CVP party.
For chairman Louis Tobback of the Flemish SP socialists the proposal was unacceptable.
He suspected some Belgians might be getting nervous as judical authorities made progress in their investigation into tax evasion and bank accounts in Luxembourg.
CVP spokesman Willy Buys said the proposed bill was not in accordance with the party's position.
Chairman Raf Vermeire of the CVP youth wing said Weyts gave a wrong signal at a time of political and financial scandals, creating the impression that tax fraud could be condoned.
He called for a more creative proposals to reduce Belgium's towering state debt and attract venture capital.

Chairman Philippe Busquin of the PS francophone socialists said the party opposed any form of fiscal amnesty. Recent fraud affairs illustrated more than ever the need for fiscal harmonisation on a European level.
The party is at the centre of scandals over kickbacks it allegedly received in the 1980s from French aviation firm Dassault and Italian helicopter maker Agusta, allegations both firms gave denied.
The alleged bribes wound up in Luxembourg bank accounts.

Another promiment case centres on a hairdresser turned call girl who inherited two billion Belgian francs ($56 million) from a tobacco chief and spirited the money away to Luxembourg, allegedly to avoid paying inheritance tax.
Last week the woman was released from custody after paying 800 million francs in bail.
Rightwing opposition party Vlaams Blok said a fiscal amnesty did not solve the core of the problem -- Belgium's high taxes which are leading to capital flight.

Chairman Herman De Croo of the VLD opposition liberals said the idea itself was good, but would founder because it created the impression it had been tailored to resolve a recent case of tax evasion involving hundreds of Luxembourg accounts.
"Still, we ought to find a way to make the billions abroad come back and be invested in new jobs," he said.
